title: Carbon capture and storage

definition.text: Separating carbon dioxide from industrial sources before it reaches the air and moving it to long-term storage, usually deep underground; known as CCS.

facts.text: Around 80% of captured CO2 is used for enhanced oil recovery, so CCS is also called carbon capture, utilization and storage (CCUS).
Capture usually passes exhaust through an amine solvent that binds CO2.
As of 2023 CCS captured around 0.1% of global emissions, about 45 million tonnes of CO2.
Capture costs US$15–25 per tonne for concentrated streams such as gas processing but US$40–120 for dilute streams from power, cement and steel plants.
Compared with other ways to cut emissions it is very expensive; many options cost under US$20 per tonne.
Site-specific designs limit cost cuts through learning-by-doing.
The literature gives CCS a small but critical role, while fossil fuel companies promote it to extend the fossil era, making it politically divisive.

related: Bioenergy with carbon capture and storage
contested_note: CCS remains politically divisive, with disagreement over its cost-effectiveness and whether it prolongs fossil fuel use.

title: Enhanced oil recovery with captured CO2
article: Carbon capture and storage#Emissions with enhanced oil recovery

definition.text: Injecting captured CO2 into old oil fields to push out more oil, and the dispute over whether this helps or harms the climate.

facts.text: Counting the emissions from burning the extra oil, capture with EOR usually increases total emissions; leaving them out, it reduces them.
A 2020 review found scientific papers roughly evenly split on the question.
The IEA estimates 80% of EOR oil displaces other oil, giving 0.13 tonnes of CO2 from burning per tonne stored.

contested_note: Studies are split on whether CO2-based enhanced oil recovery raises or lowers net emissions.

title: Energy penalty of CCS
article: Carbon capture and storage#Energy and water requirements

definition.text: The extra energy a facility uses to capture, compress and store its CO2.

facts.text: Early studies found a coal plant needs 14–40% more coal and a gas plant 11–22% more gas for the same electricity.
Burning more fuel raises upstream harms such as mining and methane leaks, and can increase local air pollution.
Coal plants with CCS may need 50% more water.

title: Unabated fossil fuels
article: Carbon capture and storage#Fossil fuel abatement

definition.text: Fossil fuels burned without measures, such as carbon capture, that substantially cut their emissions.

facts.text: Negotiators have argued over phasing out all fossil fuels or only 'unabated' ones.
The 2023 UN climate conference agreed to phase down unabated coal but left 'abated' undefined, which critics say invites abuse.
The IPCC counts power plants as abated only if they capture 90% or more of emissions.

contested_note: Countries disagree whether phase-out targets should cover all fossil fuels or only unabated ones.

title: Carbon capture and utilization
article: Carbon capture and storage#CO2 use in products

definition.text: Using captured CO2 as a raw material for products instead of storing it.

facts.text: As of 2022 products used only around 1% of the CO2 captured each year.
In urea fertilizer production, CO2 from the process is often recycled.

definition.text: Stopping the burning of coal in power plants and elsewhere, as part of the fossil fuel phase-out.

facts.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel; the IEA estimates it caused over 30% of warming above pre-industrial levels.
Coal power emits about a tonne of CO2 per megawatt hour, twice as much as gas.
Its health and environmental benefits exceed its costs, by over 1% of GDP a year according to one estimate.
Economists have suggested a Coasean bargain in which developed countries help pay for developing countries' coal phase-out.
The IEA 1.5°C pathway would require closing around 70% of existing coal capacity early.
Germany uses reverse auctions to pay coal plants to close early, and some countries retire coal miners early as part of a just transition.
Coal phase-down was agreed in the 2021 Glasgow Climate Pact.

definition.text: The point of highest coal consumption, after which use is expected to decline.

facts.text: Once expected to come from running out of reserves, peak coal is now driven by falling demand as climate policy and cheaper gas and renewables spread.
Coal's share of global energy peaked in 2008 at 30%.
Use is falling in the US and Europe but rising in India, Indonesia and China.
